label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
Dear Mr Obi, Esq., Keeper of Other People's Costings,

I'm writing because you said that if I was serious I should put it in writing, and you know I can't resist a challenge from you. So here it is. Don't read it on your phone, read it properly, with tea, like a grown man who has been bored for nine years.

I'll start with the thing you'll find most annoying, which is that you're good at this. Properly good. Do you remember Moremi before exams? Half the hostel was knocking on your door with their past papers, and you were explaining things to people who'd been ignoring their lecturers all term, and you never once made anyone feel stupid for asking. You'd just sit there, patient as anything, until it clicked. You got an A in further maths and you still treated it like it was nothing. Some people spend their whole lives trying to be able to explain something clearly. You do it without thinking.

Then there's Christmas. You sat my nephew down with a plate of jollof and some fried plantain and sorted out fractions with portions. He still talks about it. He tells people "Uncle Kel's rice maths." He is nine. He has no idea that's the exact thing teachers spend whole careers trying to do, and you just did it over the dinner table because he was bored and you were bored and it was a good way to pass the time.

Now the bit I actually want to tell you about, because it's why I've been thinking about this since your birthday. Last month, a Year 11 lad called Damola got simultaneous equations. He'd been stuck on them for three weeks. Three weeks of me going over the same thing and him going quiet and pretending he was fine. Then one Tuesday, it just clicked for him. He looked up, went "is that all??" and the whole class clapped. Not because I told them to. Because he'd got it and they'd watched him get it. I went home and sat in the car for twenty minutes just thinking about it. That's the thing I'm trying to describe to you. I don't know another job where you get that kind of moment every single week.

Right. Now I'm going to be honest, because you'll stop listening the minute I start selling it.

The first year pays less. Yes, that's the truth. You'd be earning less than you are now while you train, and I'm not going to pretend that doesn't matter, because you have to pay rent and you're not twenty-two anymore. What you get in exchange is that you're paid while you train. It's a proper salaried route, not you stacking up debt and hoping. You also get holidays, a pension, and the pay goes up after that first year. It's not nothing. But it's a real drop and you'd need to sit down with a calculator and your actual numbers. You're good with numbers, you'll have it done in twenty minutes.

The marking is endless. I'm not kidding. There are some weeks where I'm on my laptop at eleven at night going through books and wondering where my life went. You'll get kids who don't want to be in the room, and some days the behaviour is pure wahala. Some lessons go badly and you go home feeling like you did nothing right. I'm not going to paper over any of that. You'd find out in week two anyway, and then you'd think I'd lied to you.

When I started in 2019, I cried in the car park twice in my first term. Twice. I'm not hiding that from you, because it's the part people don't say. But it got better. Not all at once. It got better in the way you get better at anything, slowly, then one day you realise you've stopped dreading Monday mornings and started looking forward to a particular group. Now I can't imagine doing anything else. I'm not saying that to convince you it'll be easy. I'm saying it because the bad bit ends.

And about being too old, because I know you're going to say it. You're thirty-four. There's a woman in my department who started teaching at forty-one, and she's now the best teacher I know. Her Year 10s would walk through fire for her. You'd be starting at thirty-five with nine years of working life behind you, which means you know how grown-ups behave in meetings, how to deal with difficult people, how to keep calm when things go wrong. Those are things a lot of twenty-two-year-old trainees have to learn the hard way. You'd have them already.

Here's what I think is going on, and you can tell me I'm wrong. On your last birthday you said, "I just want to do something that matters before I'm forty." You said it half-joking, you were on your second drink, and then you changed the subject. But I heard you. I've known you since Unilag. You were never someone who wanted to check other people's costings for the rest of your life. You were the one explaining the maths to everyone else in the room. And I don't think it's a coincidence that the thing you're best at, you've been doing for free for years, and the thing you do for money, you describe to me as the same spreadsheet every day.

So I'm not asking you to quit anything or sign anything. I'm not asking you to decide this month. I'm asking you to come to the open evening. It's on Thursday 19 November 2026, 6pm, at the training partnership in Lewisham. Come and look at the place, ask them the awkward questions about money and workload and what the first year actually looks like. Ask to speak to someone who's done the route. If you hate it, you go home and we go to Nando's and I never mention it again. If you don't hate it, then at least you've made the decision with your eyes open, instead of wondering for the next five years.

I'll come with you. I'll even pay for the train, which I know is a big deal for you because you once made me pay for your chips at Peckham Rye and told me it was a loan.

Please just go and have a look. That's all I'm asking. And if you still think it's a bad idea after that, I'll buy you a proper dinner and you can tell me I was wrong, which you will enjoy far too much.

Love,

[Your name]

P.S. I'm still annoyed you didn't reply to the voice note from last year. You owe me one.

---

Post this first class so it lands before the 19th. Text him the date and time too, so he doesn't read the letter, put it down, and forget.
